rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient spanning nearly the full solvent-strength range at a mid temperature to reveal overall retention spread, possible late eluters, and whether the sample is broadly or tightly distributed. A 20 min gradient balances coverage and information density for the first run.

All 10 compounds eluted with excellent resolution, so the next step is to shorten the gradient to reduce the time penalty while checking whether the closest cluster around rows 5–7 remains adequately resolved. Keeping composition range and temperature fixed isolates the effect of gradient time.

The 14 min gradient is very fast but slightly under-resolves the critical pair, so increase tG modestly to recover separation while likely keeping the run short enough to preserve an excellent CRF. Holding phi0, phi1, and T constant continues the focused optimization around the promising region.

Since 14 min gave the best CRF but slightly under-resolved the critical pair and 16 min restored full resolution with only a small time penalty, 18 min tests whether the response is flat or worsening on the slower side. This helps confirm whether 14 min is truly optimal or whether added robustness could come at little cost.

The optimum is clearly near tG 14–16 min, so now probe temperature as a selective lever to improve the critical pair at the faster 14 min gradient without increasing run time. A modest 5 C decrease is a conservative first test for changing relative retention in the crowded mid-elution region.

Lowering temperature worsened selectivity markedly, so test the opposite direction at the fast 14 min gradient to see whether a modest temperature increase improves the crowded mid-region and the critical pair without sacrificing the zero time penalty. This is the most informative one-factor follow-up around the current best method.

Temperature changes at 14 min strongly altered selectivity, so combine the selectivity shift from 35 C with the gentler 16 min gradient that already resolved the critical region at 40 C. This tests whether added gradient time can rescue the compressed pair pattern seen at lower temperature while maintaining a competitive CRF.

Temperature variation was detrimental, so now test a small increase in phi0 at the best tG and T to selectively compress the earliest, over-resolved peaks and potentially redistribute spacing in the crowded mid-elution cluster. This keeps the fast method while probing whether gradient start composition can improve the critical pair without extending runtime.

Raising phi0 from 0.05 to 0.10 improved CRF and slightly improved the critical pair while shortening the run, so continue in the same direction with phi0 0.15 to see if the crowded mid-region benefits further. This is a focused local search around the new best condition.

Phi0 = 0.10 is currently best, and the key remaining limitation is the slightly weak 6/7 separation; increasing tG from 14 to 16 min at this improved phi0 may lift that pair above the threshold with only a small time penalty. This is the most promising nearby tradeoff to test against the current best CRF.

The best method appears to be the combination of phi0 = 0.10 and tG = 16 min, but phi0 = 0.15 was nearly as good at 14 min and gave a shorter chromatogram. Testing phi0 = 0.15 at 16 min checks whether the extra gradient time can recover full resolution with an even lower time cost, potentially improving on the current optimum.

A perfect CRF has already been reached, so this run should map the plateau around the optimum and look for an equally perfect but potentially more robust nearby condition. Increasing phi0 one more step is the most logical local test because that trend shortened the chromatogram while maintaining strong selectivity up to now.

With a perfect method already found, test whether reducing phi1 slightly preserves full resolution while trimming the high-organic end and possibly improving robustness or final hold behavior without lengthening the run. This is a small local perturbation around the optimum that probes sensitivity of the late peak spacing to gradient endpoint.

The optimum is likely on a narrow plateau near phi0 0.15, so test a slightly longer gradient at the best phi0 to see whether CRF remains perfect and how much robustness margin exists around the critical pair. This confirms whether injection 11 is a sharp optimum or part of a broad stable region.

Since lowering phi1 to 0.90 preserved full resolution with only a slight time cost, take one more step down in phi1 at the proven optimal phi0 and tG to locate the endpoint boundary of the perfect region. This probes whether a lower gradient end still keeps all compounds eluting quickly enough while maintaining the critical pair separation.

A perfect CRF has already been achieved, so use remaining injections to test robustness around the optimum. A small temperature increase at the best composition and gradient checks whether injection 11 is uniquely optimal or whether an equally strong nearby operating point exists.

Higher and lower temperatures have both hurt selectivity in related runs, but 30 C at the optimal composition/gradient cleanly brackets the temperature sensitivity around the perfect 40 C method. This final temperature check will define robustness and confirm whether 40 C is a true local optimum.

The best region is clearly centered at 40 C and tG 16 min, so this run probes a neighboring composition point combining the strong performers phi0 0.10 and phi1 0.90. It maps the local plateau around the optimum and checks whether another fully resolved zero-time-penalty condition exists.

With the global optimum already secured, use a remaining run to separate the effects of temperature and gradient steepness near the best composition. This tests whether the severe temperature sensitivity seen at 16 min persists at the faster 14 min gradient or if a useful alternative operating point exists.

No tested neighbor has beaten the optimum, so use a remaining injection to complete the local response surface at the other strong phi0 level. This checks whether phi0 0.10 with a slightly longer gradient offers a comparable fully resolved plateau or confirms that phi0 0.15, tG 16 is uniquely best.

With the optimum already found, the remaining value is in defining the nearby boundary of acceptable conditions. This steeper, lower-endpoint gradient tests how far phi1 can be reduced at phi0 0.15 while keeping all compounds eluting and may reveal whether the perfect method sits near a broad practical window.

The 0.15/0.80 composition window looks promising, and reducing tG from 16 to 14 still preserved full resolution with only a tiny time penalty. Testing 12 min probes whether this lower phi1 can support an even faster fully resolved method, potentially matching the optimum from a different direction.

The lower-phi1 region remains strong, so take one more step down in phi1 at 14 min to define the edge of the high-performing plateau. This should show whether the current optimum is part of a broader practical family of methods or whether selectivity begins to collapse below phi1 0.80.

With two injections left and the optimum already secured, probe one unexplored corner near the best region that combines higher phi0 with a slightly reduced phi1 at the faster 14 min gradient. This helps map whether a distinct short, strong-gradient family can approach the optimum or whether selectivity consistently degrades when phi0 is pushed higher.

For the final run, probe the remaining untested composition point between the strong 0.10/0.95 and 0.15/0.80 neighborhoods to complete the local map near the optimum. This may reveal another high-scoring short method while confirming how phi0 and phi1 trade off around the critical pair.
